title: What PPE training does OSHA require under 1910.132?
description: OSHA 1910.132(f) PPE training: five knowledge points, demonstration before work, retraining triggers and which records apply, as at November 2026.
shortAnswer: The Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) standard 29 CFR 1910.132(f) requires employers to train each employee who must use personal protective equipment (PPE) in when PPE is necessary, what PPE is necessary, how to don, doff, adjust and wear it, its limitations, and its care, useful life and disposal. Each employee must demonstrate understanding and the ability to use PPE properly before doing the work, and must be retrained when changes or knowledge gaps make earlier training obsolete.
keyTakeaways: Training follows the hazard assessment: paragraph (d)(1) requires the employer to assess hazards and select PPE before (f) training content can be defined.
Paragraph (f)(2) makes demonstration a precondition: employees must show understanding and the ability to use PPE properly before being allowed to perform work requiring it.
There is no fixed refresher interval; (f)(3) requires retraining on workplace changes, PPE changes, or inadequate knowledge or use.
The current text of 1910.132 requires a written certification of the hazard assessment under (d)(2), but contains no paragraph requiring a training certification.
Paragraphs (d) and (f) apply to eye and face, head, foot and hand protection and personal fall protection systems, not to respirators (1910.134) or electrical protective equipment (1910.137).
jurisdiction: United States (federal, with state plan variations)
regulator: Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA), US Department of Labor
appliesTo: General industry employers whose hazard assessment identifies hazards requiring PPE
Employees required to use eye and face, head, foot or hand protection, or personal fall protection systems
Supervisors who verify PPE use and identify retraining needs

sections.heading: Why does PPE training start with the hazard assessment?

blocks.text: PPE training content depends on the hazard assessment, so the assessment must exist first. Paragraph (d)(1) of [29 CFR 1910.132](https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/regulations/standardnumber/1910/1910.132) requires the employer to assess the workplace to determine whether hazards are present, or likely to be present, that necessitate PPE. Where they are, the employer must select the types of PPE that protect against the identified hazards and have each affected employee use them, communicate selection decisions to each affected employee, and select PPE that properly fits each affected employee.

Paragraph (d)(2) requires a written certification that the hazard assessment was performed, identifying the workplace evaluated, the person certifying, the dates of the assessment, and that the document is a certification of hazard assessment. That certification is the anchor document for PPE training: it names the hazards and the PPE that the training must explain.

sections.heading: What must each employee be trained to know?

blocks.text: Paragraph (f)(1) requires training for each employee required by the section to use PPE, so that each such employee knows at least five things:

items: How to properly don, doff, adjust and wear PPE.
The proper care, maintenance, useful life and disposal of the PPE.

blocks.text: The list is generic, but the content cannot be. "When" and "what" come from the hazard assessment for the employee's specific tasks. Limitations and useful life come from the manufacturer's information for the PPE actually issued. A generic video on safety glasses does not tell an employee which tasks in their area require a face shield as well.

sections.heading: What does demonstration of understanding require?

blocks.text: Each affected employee must demonstrate both understanding and practical ability before working. Paragraph (f)(2) states that each affected employee "shall demonstrate an understanding of the training specified in paragraph (f)(1) of this section, and the ability to use PPE properly, before being allowed to perform work requiring the use of PPE."

Two kinds of evidence answer that sentence. Understanding can be shown by a short assessment on the five knowledge points for the employee's own tasks. Ability to use PPE properly needs observation: a supervisor watching the employee don, adjust and doff the equipment, or a practical check during the first shift. The order matters, because the demonstration must come before the work.

blocks.title: Sequence an auditor will test
blocks.text: Hazard assessment certified, PPE selected and fitted, training delivered on the five points, understanding and ability demonstrated, then work authorized. A start date that precedes the demonstration date is a finding under (f)(2).

sections.heading: When must PPE training be repeated?

blocks.text: PPE retraining is event driven, not annual. Paragraph (f)(3) requires the employer to retrain any trained employee whom it has reason to believe lacks the understanding and skill required by (f)(2). It lists three circumstances, while stating that retraining is "not limited to" them:

items: Changes in the workplace render previous training obsolete.
Changes in the types of PPE to be used render previous training obsolete.
Inadequacies in an affected employee's knowledge or use of assigned PPE indicate that the employee has not retained the requisite understanding or skill.

blocks.text: The "reason to believe" standard means supervisors' observations are part of the system. An employee seen wearing gloves unsuitable for the chemical in use is a retraining trigger, and the record of that observation and the follow-up training is the evidence. Standards with fixed annual cycles, such as [OSHA respiratory protection](/regulations/osha-respiratory-protection-training-requirements) and [OSHA hearing conservation](/regulations/osha-hearing-conservation-training-requirements), cover PPE that falls outside 1910.132(f).

sections.heading: Which PPE does 1910.132(f) cover, and what records are required?

blocks.text: Paragraph (g) limits the hazard assessment and training paragraphs to five sections: 1910.133 (eye and face protection), 1910.135 (head protection), 1910.136 (foot protection), 1910.138 (hand protection) and 1910.140 (personal fall protection systems). It states that (d) and (f) do not apply to 1910.134 (respiratory protection) or 1910.137 (electrical protective equipment), which have their own provisions.

On records, the current text of 1910.132 as published on osha.gov and in the eCFR has three training paragraphs, (f)(1) to (f)(3), and no paragraph requiring a training certification. The only written certification in the section is the hazard assessment certification in (d)(2). Employers still need evidence that (f)(2) demonstrations happened before work began, but the format is the employer's choice. Standards that do prescribe training certifications, such as lockout/tagout and powered industrial trucks, are compared in [OSHA recordkeeping and training documentation](/regulations/osha-recordkeeping-and-training-documentation).

sections.heading: Who pays for PPE and how is the standard enforced?

blocks.text: The employer pays for PPE used to comply with part 1910, with listed exceptions. Paragraph (h)(1) requires PPE to be provided at no cost, while (h)(2) to (h)(4) exclude non-specialty safety-toe footwear and prescription safety eyewear that employees may wear off site, logging boots, everyday clothing and ordinary weather protection. Paragraph (h)(7) records that the payment provisions became effective on February 13, 2008, with implementation required by May 15, 2008.

OSHA enforces PPE provisions through inspection. Its [preliminary top 10 for fiscal year 2026](https://www.osha.gov/top10citedstandards) lists eye and face protection in construction (1926.102) ninth across all industries, a reminder that PPE selection and training remain common findings. For designing role-based PPE curricula, see [how to build a training matrix](/guides/how-to-build-a-training-matrix) and [how to design competency assessments](/guides/how-to-design-competency-assessments). The overview of OSHA duties is at [OSHA training requirements](/regulations/osha-training-requirements).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry links the certified hazard assessment to the PPE selected for each task and to the five knowledge points, so the training for a role is generated from the assessment rather than written separately. A change to a hazard or a PPE model identifies the employees whose training is now obsolete under (f)(3).

faqs.q: Does OSHA require annual PPE training?
faqs.a: No fixed interval applies under 1910.132(f). Retraining is required when workplace or PPE changes make training obsolete or when an employee's knowledge or use shows they have not retained the required understanding or skill. Some PPE, such as respirators, carries its own annual requirement under a different standard.

faqs.q: Does OSHA require a signed PPE training certificate?
faqs.a: The current text of 1910.132 contains no paragraph requiring a training certification. It does require a written certification of the hazard assessment under (d)(2). Employers still need evidence that each employee demonstrated understanding and ability before starting work, in a format they choose.

faqs.q: Can PPE training be completed online?
faqs.a: The knowledge points can be taught online, but (f)(2) requires each employee to demonstrate the ability to use PPE properly, not only understanding. That usually requires a practical check of donning, adjusting and doffing, observed by a supervisor or trainer, before the employee starts the work.

faqs.q: Does 1910.132(f) cover respirators and arc flash clothing?
faqs.a: Paragraph (g) excludes respiratory protection under 1910.134 and electrical protective equipment under 1910.137 from the hazard assessment and training paragraphs. Those sections carry their own requirements. Paragraph (f) covers eye and face, head, foot and hand protection and personal fall protection systems.

factCheck.claim: 1910.132(d)(1): assess workplace; select PPE, communicate selection, select PPE that fits; (d)(2) written certification of hazard assessment with workplace, certifier, dates, identification as certification.

1910.132(f)(1)(i)-(v): five knowledge points; (f)(2) demonstrate understanding and ability before being allowed to perform work; (f)(3) retraining with three listed circumstances, not limited to them.

Current 1910.132 text (osha.gov, Cornell eCFR, and eCFR API point-in-time 2026-11-01) contains (f)(1)-(f)(3) only; no training certification paragraph. eCFR version history shows no change since 2017-01-18.
1910.132(h): PPE at no cost with exceptions (h)(2)-(h)(4); (h)(7) effective February 13, 2008, implement by May 15, 2008.
